---
title: "Key challenges and trade-offs"
date-modified: "2026-05-12"
---

Alternative data sources introduce a number of challenges and trade-offs
that National Statistical Offices (NSOs) must actively manage.

These considerations often cut across organisational boundaries and
require balancing competing priorities rather than identifying a single
"optimal" solution.

Importantly, many of these challenges are not purely technical. Legal
frameworks, governance arrangements, skills, and user expectations all
influence how alternative data can be used in practice.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Legal, ethical, and governance considerations {#Keychallengesandtradeoffs-Legalethicalandgovernanceconsiderations end="1026" data-start="988"}

Access to alternative data is often governed by complex legal and
contractual arrangements. Unlike survey data, where NSOs typically have
well-established legal mandates, alternative data sources may involve:

- Commercial data providers,

- Third-party intermediaries, or

- Data originally collected for non-statistical purposes.

NSOs must assess whether [data access is legally
sustainable](data-sharing-agreements.qmd) over time, whether
terms of use permit statistical reuse, and how risks related to
confidentiality, privacy, and ethical use are managed. These
considerations may constrain methodological choices or limit how results
can be published or shared.

# Stability, continuity, and dependency risks {#Keychallengesandtradeoffs-Stabilitycontinuityanddependencyrisks end="1790" data-start="1743"}

Alternative data sources may be subject to changes outside the control
of the NSO. For example:

- Retailers may change product identifiers or reporting practices,

- Websites may alter structure or restrict automated access or even be
  discontinued,

- Data providers may discontinue or modify data deliveries.

These risks create a trade-off between innovation and robustness. Highly
detailed or novel data sources may offer analytical benefits but
increase vulnerability to supply disruptions, requiring contingency
planning.

# Methodological complexity versus transparency {#Keychallengesandtradeoffs-Methodologicalcomplexityversustransparency end="2366" data-start="2317"}

Many alternative data sources enable the use of more sophisticated index
methods. While these methods may offer desirable statistical properties,
they can also:

- Increase computational and system complexity,

- Build the team skills to learn and use such methods;

- Be harder to explain to non-technical users, and

- Complicate internal validation and quality assurance processes.

NSOs must balance methodological refinement with transparency,
reproducibility, and the need to maintain trust in official statistics.
In some cases, simpler methods may be preferred during early
[implementation phases](implementation.qmd), even if more
advanced approaches are planned longer term.

# Timeliness versus revision policy {#Keychallengesandtradeoffs-Timelinessversusrevisionpolicy end="3010" data-start="2973"}

Some alternative data based methods, particularly multilateral index
approaches, may imply revisions when new data become available. This can
conflict with established CPI revision policies or user expectations of
non-revised headline indices.

NSOs therefore face trade-offs between:

- Using methods that make full use of available data, and

- Maintaining stable, non-revised published series.

Splicing, window design, and publication strategies become critical
choices in managing this tension. These are discussed further in [Price
index methods](price-index-methods.qmd). 

# Resource constraints and skill requirements {#Keychallengesandtradeoffs-Resourceconstraintsandskillrequirements end="3556" data-start="3509"}

Although alternative data sources have the potential to reduce long-term
costs, their adoption typically requires upfront investment. This may
include:

- New IT infrastructure,

- Data engineering and coding skills,

- Methodological expertise in advanced index number theory, and

- Ongoing maintenance capacity.

NSOs must consider whether these resources are available internally,
whether partnerships are required, and how knowledge is retained over
time.

# Organisational coordination and change management {#Keychallengesandtradeoffs-Organisationalcoordinationandchangemanagement end="4069" data-start="4016"}

Introducing alternative data often affects multiple parts of the
organisation simultaneously. For example, data acquisition, IT systems,
methodology teams, and dissemination units may all need to adapt.

A key trade-off is between incremental integration, where new data
sources are phased in gradually, and more transformative approaches that
redesign production systems end-to-end. Both approaches have merits, but
they imply different risks, timelines, and management challenges.

These challenges and trade-offs mean that adopting alternative data
sources is not simply a technical exercise. NSOs must make a series of
deliberate decisions about scope, methods, governance, and resourcing.
